title: Speech Privacy in Buildings
journal: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
classification_signals: Methods section present with laboratory study design
Results section with experimental data and tables
Sample sizes reported for test subjects
Field study with case histories (37 buildings)
research_question: What is the relationship between speech privacy in buildings and the physical characteristics of room isolation, background noise, and speech intelligibility? Can a rating scheme be developed to predict occupant satisfaction with speech privacy?

hypotheses.statement: Speech privacy is related to the ratio of the intruding speech to the background noise level rather than the level of the speech itself
A scheme based on articulation index (AI) can accurately predict occupant satisfaction with speech privacy
Background noise level significantly influences the intelligibility of intruding speech

findings.antecedent: speech level ratio (intruding speech level minus background noise level) at approximately 10 dB or greater
findings.consequent: occupant perception of speech privacy as inadequate (high intelligibility of intruding speech)

scope_unknown_dimensions: generalization to other building types beyond offices

findings.mechanism: High speech-to-noise ratio allows acoustic energy of intruding speech to exceed the masking threshold of background noise, enabling word recognition and comprehension by listeners

mechanism_chain.from_construct: intruding speech level minus background noise level

moderators_reported: type of speech content (sentences vs. syllables)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Speech intelligibility depends on the ratio of speech signal to background noise, with the articulation index as a quantitative measure

components.name: intruding speech
components.details: Recorded speech played through loudspeaker in adjacent office or test room at controlled levels

components.name: background noise
components.details: Steady background noise in listening room at controlled levels (NC contours ranging from NC-30 to NC-50)

stimulus_description.stimulus_image_description: Figures 1, 7 show test setup with loudspeaker in talker's room, sound transmission through wall, and measurement apparatus in listener's room. Figure 5 shows graphical representation of normal sound levels in a 100-dB office room.

findings.source: Section V: Experiments on the Relationship Between Speech Intelligibility and Speech Privacy, Figure 9 and text discussion
findings.quote: One possible explanation for the above observations is that speech privacy is related to speech intelligibility. We found that each subject had a precise personal criterion for the speech-to-noise ratio which for him just constituted privacy

findings.antecedent: critical speech-to-noise ratio threshold (approximately 0-6 dB where AI = 0.05)
findings.consequent: shift from 'apparent satisfaction' to 'dissatisfaction' with speech privacy

scope_conditions.setting: laboratory simulation of private office environment

findings.mechanism: At critical AI threshold (0.05), speech transitions from unintelligible background to recognizable content, crossing the psychoacoustic boundary between privacy and intrusion
moderators_reported: individual variation in critical AI threshold (range 0-0.10)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: AI value of 0.05 represents the critical threshold between privacy and intrusion for architectural design purposes

components.name: variable speech level
components.details: Recorded speech level gradually increased from unintelligible to intelligible across test series

stimulus_description.stimulus_image_description: Figures 9 and 10 show results plotting AI threshold against observer response, with curves showing the transition point from satisfaction to dissatisfaction.

findings.source: Section V and VIII: Results showing relationship between AI and privacy threshold, Figure 10
findings.quote: It is significant that situations with an articulation index of 0.05 are more or less on the borderline between apparent satisfaction and some degree of dissatisfaction. Thus, if economy is of utmost importance, the design criterion should be based on this value.

findings.antecedent: transmission loss (TL) from source room to receiving room (range 30-50+ dB across different wall constructions)
findings.consequent: noise reduction (NR) rating and predicted occupant satisfaction with speech privacy (case histories)

scope_conditions.setting: field study across 37 buildings (professional offices, hospitals, dormitories, hotels, factories)
scope_conditions.population: office workers, hospital staff, students, hotel occupants, factory workers
scope_conditions.measurement_type: combined objective TL measurement and subjective occupant assessment
scope_unknown_dimensions: applicability to other climate zones or countries

findings.mechanism: Sound isolation (TL) reduces both the absolute intruding speech level and the speech-to-noise ratio, thereby decreasing intelligibility below the critical threshold for privacy perception
moderators_reported: background noise level in receiving room
source room size and sound-absorbing area
partition type (masonry, plaster, studded wall, etc.)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Sound isolation (TL) combined with background noise level and articulation index can predict occupant satisfaction with speech privacy in real buildings

components.name: partition construction
components.details: Various wall constructions tested: plaster partitions, masonry walls, wall with air leaks, studded walls with fiberglass, etc.

components.name: intruding speech activity
components.details: Normal office activity, telephone conversations, typical workplace speech

findings.antecedent: Noise Reduction (NR) rating system combining source room speech level, background noise level, and articulation index (AI = 0.05 threshold)
findings.consequent: accurate prediction of occupant satisfaction with speech privacy across diverse building types

scope_conditions.setting: field validation across 37 buildings representing diverse types
scope_conditions.population: building occupants across multiple sectors (n=37 buildings)
scope_conditions.measurement_type: combined objective measurements and subjective assessment
scope_unknown_dimensions: applicability to residential buildings not covered in sample

findings.mechanism: The NR rating scheme aggregates physical acoustic parameters (TL, background noise) into a single-number metric that predicts occupant behavior by mapping to the critical AI threshold of 0.05

mechanism_chain.from_construct: transmission loss and background noise level

mechanism_chain.to_construct: predicted articulation index at critical threshold

theory_commitments.specific_claim: NR rating operationalizes the AI threshold concept for practical building design

findings.antecedent: background noise level in receiving room (range NC-20 to NC-50 noise contours)
findings.consequent: required transmission loss (TL) value to achieve acceptable speech privacy

scope_conditions.setting: laboratory and field measurements across multiple room types
scope_conditions.population: various building types and occupant profiles

findings.mechanism: Higher background noise level masks more of the intruding speech content, reducing the effective speech-to-noise ratio and thus the articulation index; therefore, lower TL is required to achieve privacy

mechanism_chain.to_construct: required reduction in intruding speech level

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Background noise masking is a key variable in determining required sound isolation for privacy

components.name: controlled background noise
components.details: Background noise at various NC levels from NC-20 (quiet) to NC-50 (noisy)

components.name: intruding speech
components.details: Recorded speech at standard levels played through partition

findings.source: Section IV: Other Factors Important to Speech Privacy; Figures 2 and 4
findings.quote: The degree of speech privacy required by the occupant of a room depends on his activity. As an example, consider the case of an engineer or other technical person. During most of his work day, his desire for speech isolation is set by his wish for freedom from distraction.

findings.antecedent: lower background noise level in listening room (range NC-20 to NC-35)
findings.consequent: greater required change in intruding speech level to reach privacy satisfaction threshold

scope_unknown_dimensions: generalization to field environments with dynamic noise

findings.mechanism: Lower background noise reduces masking of intruding speech, making the same speech content more intelligible; therefore a greater reduction in speech level is needed to reach the critical AI threshold

mechanism_chain.to_construct: speech level adjustment needed for privacy

moderators_reported: individual subject variation in privacy threshold

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Masking is the primary mechanism by which background noise influences speech privacy perception

components.name: variable background noise level
components.details: NC-20 to NC-35 background noise levels controlled in test chamber

components.name: intruding speech recording
components.details: Recorded speech played at adjustable levels through loudspeaker

findings.source: Section V: Experiments, subsection (1) Background Noise; Figures 5 and 9
findings.quote: The intelligibility of intruding speech is destroyed when the speech peaks are not exceeded in intensity by steady background noise (or when reduced below the threshold of hearing—thus, an increase in the background level has the same effect on intelligibility as an increase in the transmission loss.

limitations: Laboratory studies limited to simulated office environment; field validation through case histories may not capture all real-world acoustic variability
Sample of 13 test subjects may not represent all occupant populations with different noise sensitivity or privacy expectations
Case history data from 37 buildings is primarily office-focused; generalization to residential or industrial settings uncertain
Individual variation in privacy criteria (AI threshold range 0-0.10) not fully accounted for in single-number NR rating scheme
Long-time variability of subjects' responses not explored; may be adaptive learning effects over time
Background noise spectrum assumed to follow NC criteria; real-world noise may have different spectral characteristics
Field data collection methods varied across buildings; standardization limitations
